products.name: Krea AI
products.note: Real-time video generation; creative tool; content moderation; emerging platform

reading.body:
Krea aggregates third-party video and image generation models from ByteDance, Google, Minimax, and Alibaba into a single creative interface, rather than building its own foundation models.

The platform's strategy is access, not infrastructure. Users can generate real-time video at resolutions up to 2K and images at 4K through models they could not reach individually. Krea surfaces Seedance variants from ByteDance, Veo and Gemini models from Google, Minimax's frontier video model, and Alibaba's video capabilities alongside web search and code execution tools for specialized tasks like rendering charts and QR codes. This is an aggregation play in a field increasingly defined by model proliferation.

For AI deployment, this matters because it shows the shift from monolithic platforms to composable ones. Users no longer choose a single vendor's video model. They choose an interface that routes requests to whichever model fits the task. The compute cost moves downstream to the model providers, while Krea absorbs infrastructure costs for serving inference at real-time latency. Whether real-time video generation at scale strains the grid depends on user volume and inference frequency, neither of which this data covers.

The data does not include Krea's funding, user count, compute infrastructure location, or power consumption. It does not explain why these particular models were selected or how their inference loads are distributed. It records what Krea offers, not what it costs to run.

profile_text.body:
Krea describes itself as a creative AI suite for generating, editing, and enhancing images and videos, and says it can be used for free. Its website lists a single tracked product, Krea AI, in the video generation and editing category, noted for real-time video generation, content moderation, and as an emerging platform. The company is headquartered in San Francisco.

The site presents Krea as a hub for third-party generative models rather than a single in-house model. The video models it lists include ByteDance's flagship video model, described as producing 30-second clips at up to 1080p with 20% better prompt adherence, native synchronized audio, tagged image, video, and audio references, region-level editing, and frame animation; a Minimax frontier model rendering at 2K; Google's video-first multimodal model; ByteDance Seedance 2.0 Mini; Google's Gemini Omni video model; Black Forest Labs' video editing model, which accepts clips up to 15 seconds; and Alibaba's latest generation video model, with clips up to 30 seconds at up to 1080p and up to 10 reference images, 5 reference videos, and 5 reference audios. FLUX 3 is described as one model across image, video, and audio that renders up to 20 seconds in a single pass.

On the image side, the site lists Google's latest flash image model, also known as Gemini 3.1 Flash Image, optimized for fast generation at up to 4K; a flagship ByteDance model with local edits, multi-image fusion, and up to 10 reference images; Muse Image, which plans before rendering and supports composition from up to 10 images; Alibaba's third-generation image model, reading prompts up to 4.5k tokens and rendering text down to 10px across 12 languages; a model that generates and edits with native transparency; and a latest Qwen model with enhanced human realism. No lawsuits, SEC filings, patents, or MCP servers are recorded for the company.
